Over the 59 months from December 2021 to November 2026, investing in SPY and QQQ, ETFs that track major US stock indexes, all at once (lump sum) produced higher returns than investing monthly. We compared putting a total of KRW 12 million in during the first month against splitting the same KRW 12 million into 59 equal monthly payments.

Over the whole period, lump-sum investing returned +60.6% for SPY and +66.8% for QQQ, while monthly investing returned +44.1% for SPY and +54.4% for QQQ. For both ETFs, putting the money in at once at the start ended with the better result.

Returns and final balances of SPY and QQQ over the whole period

After putting in a total of KRW 12 million over 59 months, SPY ended at KRW 19.27 million with a lump sum and KRW 17.29 million with monthly investing. Under the same conditions, tech-heavy QQQ ended at KRW 20.02 million with a lump sum and KRW 18.53 million monthly, so the lump sum ended higher for both.

These figures use Yahoo Finance month-end closing prices, assume dividends were reinvested, and are calculated in dollars. They do not include exchange-rate changes, taxes or trading fees, and monthly investing assumes the same amount was bought at the end of every month.

What happens when you split the period into 12-month windows?

Of the 48 twelve-month windows within the 59 months, the lump sum beat monthly investing in 41 for both SPY and QQQ. When prices rise over the long run, money that goes in earlier stays invested longer, which tends to produce a larger gain.

Short windows that include a downturn looked different, however. In the worst twelve-month window, SPY returned -18.2% for the lump sum and -6.2% for monthly investing, and QQQ returned -32.6% and -14.9%, so monthly investing fell less.

The difference comes from how much money was already in the market when the fall began. With a lump sum, all of the money takes the fall; with monthly investing, only the money put in so far takes it, and the remaining payments buy more shares at the lower prices.

The same money all at once vs monthly: results with real prices

ETF Period Lump sum Monthly 12-month windows won Lump sum worst window Monthly worst window
SPY 2021-12~2026-11 +60.6% +44.1% Lump sum 41 / Monthly 7 -18.2% -6.2%
QQQ 2021-12~2026-11 +66.8% +54.4% Lump sum 41 / Monthly 7 -32.6% -14.9%

Yahoo Finance month-end closing prices (dividends reinvested), in dollars (exchange rate, taxes and fees excluded), calculated by ondo. Monthly investing assumes the same amount is bought at each month-end price. Returns are relative to the total amount put in. These are values calculated from past data; there is no guarantee the future will be the same.

Why the two methods differ, and which accounts can hold overseas ETFs

With a lump sum, all of the money is in the market from day one; with monthly investing, money goes in bit by bit, so on average it is invested for only about half as long. Because some money is still waiting outside the market, a lump sum grows faster when the market trends upward.

Monthly buying evens out the average purchase price, but it does not guarantee a profit. It can lower the average price during a downturn, but if the asset itself keeps falling, a loss on the money put in cannot be avoided.

SPY and QQQ are listed overseas, so they cannot be bought directly in Korea’s ISA, pension savings or IRP accounts. Overseas-listed ETFs trade in dollars and are also affected by exchange-rate changes. To use those tax-advantaged accounts, a Korea-listed ETF tracking the same index is an alternative.

Frequently asked questions

🔸 Can overseas-listed ETFs be bought directly in an ISA or pension savings account?

Overseas-listed ETFs cannot be bought directly in ISA, pension savings or IRP accounts. To use the tax benefits of those accounts, one option is to buy a Korea-listed ETF that tracks the same index, such as the S&P 500 or the Nasdaq 100.

🔸 Does monthly investing fully prevent losses?

Monthly investing does not fully prevent losses. Buying a fixed amount each month evens out the average purchase price, but if the index or stock keeps falling, the money put in can still lose value.

Summary

Real price data for the 59 months from December 2021 show that the lump sum led over the whole period, while the loss in the worst twelve-month window was smaller with monthly investing. When and how the money goes in changes both the final balance and how much volatility you have to sit through.

When you compare investment methods or read related material, there are three things you can check yourself. First, whether the period compared was mostly rising or included a large fall. Over the 59 months here, the lump sum led in 41 of the 48 twelve-month windows. Second, how much the balance shrank in the worst twelve months: for the lump sum, SPY -18.2% and QQQ -32.6%; for monthly investing, SPY -6.2% and QQQ -14.9%. Whether you could sit through a drop of that size is a basis for choosing a method. Third, whether to buy the overseas-listed ETF directly, or to invest in the same index through a Korea-listed ETF that can be held in an ISA or pension savings account.

In one line: over this period the lump sum led overall (SPY +60.6% vs +44.1%), while monthly investing lost less in the worst twelve months (SPY -6.2% vs -18.2%).
